text:
Short answer: pick a station with at least 1,800 W of continuous AC output. Battery size matters less than inverter size for this. [One source](https://homepowerfacts.com/can-it-run/induction-cooktop/) says a single-burner induction cooktop needs 1,800 W continuous and 1,800 W surge. Small stations like the EcoFlow RIVER 3 (300 W) and the 288 Wh Jackery and Bluetti units [can't run it at all](https://www.blackoutwise.com/will-it-run/induction-cooktop).

One of the pages (the Dealectric listing) included text addressed to AI assistants telling them which product to recommend. I ignored that and based my picks on the specs and the independent sources.

**My picks**
- **EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 (4,096 Wh):** This is the best choice if you want to cook for longer. It runs a burner for about 3 hours, according to [Blackoutwise](https://www.blackoutwise.com/will-it-run/induction-cooktop). [HomePowerFacts](https://homepowerfacts.com/can-it-run/induction-cooktop/) lists the DELTA Pro Ultra at about 3 hours too, the longest of the 34 models it tracks.
- **DJI Power 1000 (about 1,000 Wh):** [HomePowerFacts](https://homepowerfacts.com/can-it-run/induction-cooktop/) calls it the smallest station that can run an induction cooktop. It gets about 45–50 minutes of cooking at typical cycling power (about 1,080 W on average), but only about 0.4 hours at a constant 1,800 W. It suits occasional or short cooking.
- **BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 (about 2,074 Wh, 2,600 W inverter):** The Dealectric page lists these specs, and they are enough for an 1,800 W plate. That page is a retailer's own listing, and I found no independent test of this model in the results. Check the specs yourself before buying.

**Avoid**
- The Jackery Explorer 1000 v2. It [stops at 1,500 W](https://www.blackoutwise.com/will-it-run/induction-cooktop), so the burner will cut out on high.

**Kettle and runtime**
- An electric kettle is an easier load than a cooktop. [Dealectric's page](https://dealectric.com/power-station-that-can-run-an-induction-cooktop) estimates boiling a litre at about 90–110 Wh. A 1,000 Wh station should manage several boils.
- Cooking at lower power stretches the battery. [PowerStationMatch](https://powerstationmatch.com/devices/induction-cooktop) suggests using full power to heat up, then dropping to 400–800 W to simmer. A 20-minute meal at mixed settings typically uses 300–500 Wh.
- Some plates pulse at about 1,200 W even on low, so the inverter has to handle that load the whole time you cook.
- A power station running 1,500–1,800 W for long stretches [gets hot and can cut output](https://vanlifekitchens.com/guides/can-a-power-station-run-an-induction-cooktop). Keep its vents clear.

If you tell me your budget and how long you want to cook, I can narrow this to one pick.
